column4: The Next image optimizer accepts any https host so anyone can make the server fetch arbitrary URLs
column5: next.config.ts configures images.remotePatterns as a single entry of protocol https with hostname ** which is a wildcard matching every host. The optimizer endpoint takes the target in a query parameter so /_next/image?url=<any https url>&w=64&q=75 makes the storefront server issue a server side request to whatever host the caller names. Tested against a running dev server: an arbitrary external https URL was accepted and the fetch attempted - the response was 403 from this environment egress proxy rather than the 400 that Next returns for a host outside the allowlist - while an http URL to a loopback address returned that 400 so the protocol restriction is the only bound actually in force. images.dangerouslyAllowSVG is also true which means SVG payloads are processed rather than refused - the accompanying contentDispositionType of attachment does mitigate the inline execution half by forcing a download rather than a render.

column12: 1. Request /_next/image with a url parameter naming an arbitrary external https host plus w and q. 2. Observe the server attempts the fetch rather than rejecting the host. 3. Compare against an http URL which returns the Next 400 for a disallowed target.
column13: Only hosts the storefront actually serves images from are accepted - an explicit allowlist of the panel media domains and any CDN in use.
column14: Every https host on the internet is accepted and fetched by the server.
column15: The storefront server can be induced to make outbound requests to caller chosen hosts which is a server side request forgery primitive - bounded here because only https is allowed and only a successful image decode is returned to the caller. It also works as an open image proxy so a third party can serve their bandwidth through this domain and fill its optimizer cache.
column16: Replace the ** wildcard with an explicit list of the media hosts actually used - the panel domain and any CDN. If a broad allowlist is genuinely required keep dangerouslyAllowSVG off unless SVG is needed and retain contentDispositionType attachment. Both changes are in next.config.ts only.
